newsitem.title: JAPAN: World shipping rates seen falling further.
newsitem.headline: World shipping rates seen falling further.

text.p: The Baltic Freight Index (BFI), the key barometer of world freight rates, may slide further because of an absence of grain cargoes and a glut of new ships, shipping industry sources said on Tuesday.
The BFI plunged to a four-year low of 1,056 points on Monday in the absence of grain cargoes for October shipment and a scarcity for September, shipping brokers said.
They said the situation would probably be aggravated with the commissioning of more ships in an overcrowded market.

"As newly-built Panamax-sized ships enter into the market this year, (the) glut is expected to stay. Dramatic recovery is unlikely until the end of this year," an analyst at Mitsui O.S.K. Lines Ltd said.
"We don't expect (a) further sharp drop, say, to the $17 (a tonne) level...Our impression is that the freight rates are to hover between $19 and $23 throughout this year," the analyst said.
"Earlier this year, we had forecasted freight rates would be on a down-trend. It was mainly due to over-supply of ship tonnage," said Kim Sang-kyun of Dooyang Line Co Ltd in South Korea.

Freight rates continued to fall to below $20 per tonne recently from about $23 this June, industry officials in Japan said. Some traders said nearby freight rates were already quoted at below $19 last week.

Recent freight cost for Panamax-size grain shipments from the U.S. Pacific Northwest to the port of Inchon in South Korea was quoted at $10 per tonne and at $20 from the U.S. Gulf, South Korean ship brokers said.
This prompted Japanese grain importers to retreat to the sidelines, waiting for freight rates to drop further, industry sources said.

"Trade houses want the freight rates to remain below $20. But ship owners are resisting such a move. This is (the) reason behind the absence of grain cargoes for October and September," an official of another shipping company said.
The bearish mood in trans-Pacific shipping would help push down the BFI market index, they said.
"Given these bearish factors of the U.S. Gulf/Japan route, we anticipate the BFI market to remain bearish in the near term," the shipping company official said.
Freight company officials in Taiwan attributed the low rates to new bulk ship capacity coming on stream in the second half of 1996.

"There are about 60 to 70 new bulk ships joining the market in the latter half of this year," said Sincere Corp spokesman Wang Huai-chun. "The freight rates have been falling mainly because of new capacity in the market."
New ships are likely to be used in grain shipping because "dirty cargo" vessels, those that haul coal and metals, are not suitable.

But the fall in world freight rates would probably not trigger a buying spree for grain and oilseeds from the region unless prices of staples like corn and soybeans also fell sharply, regional traders said.
Most countries in the region were already well-covered for their grain and oilseed requirements for the rest of the year and buying for 1997 will not appear until late October.
"Freight alone will not able to boost buying interest from Taiwan buyers," a trader in Taipei said.

"We have already bought the requirements for corn needed till next February's shipment. The plunge of the freight index will not affect our purchases," said a trader of a leading grain import company in South Korea.
